Winebibber
WINE-bib-ber
noun
From wine and the old verb bib, “to drink,” from the Latin bibere, “to drink”; hence a wine-drinker, a tippler, one habitually given to the cup — a drunkard.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

A winebibber is a wine-drinker — one who tipples, who tarries over the cup, a drunkard. The word joins wine to the old verb bib, and it names not the man who tastes but the man who cannot leave off. Solomon sets him among the company a wise son must shun: “Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh” (Pro 23:20), “for the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags” (Pro 23:21). The father draws the portrait whole — “Who hath woe? who hath sorrow?… They that tarry long at the wine” (Pro 23:29–30) — and bids the son not so much as look upon it when it is red. Isaiah pronounces the woe over it: “Woe unto them that rise up early in the morning, that they may follow strong drink” (Isa 5:11). Yet the sharpest use of the word is a slander flung at the Son of God. Christ came eating and drinking, and the scribes sneered, “Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners” (Mat 11:19; cf. Luk 7:34). He was no winebibber; He was holy, harmless, undefiled. But He would sit at a publican’s table to save a publican, and the self-righteous had no name for such mercy but a drunkard’s name. The LORD who was falsely called a winebibber is the LORD who delivers the true one.

Webster 1828 Definition

A wine-drinker; a tippler; one habitually given to wine — a drunkard.

WINEBIBBER, one who drinks much wine; a tippler; a drunkard.

From wine and bib, “to drink,” from the Latin bibere.

It names not the taster but the man who tarries long at the cup.

Solomon warns, Be not among winebibbers (Pro 23:20).

The scribes falsely called Christ a winebibber (Mat 11:19).

Key Scripture

Pro 23:20 — "Be not among winebibbers; among riotous eaters of flesh:"

Mat 11:19 — "The Son of man came eating and drinking, and they say, Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners. But wisdom is justified of her children."

Luk 7:34 — "The Son of man is come eating and drinking; and ye say, Behold a gluttonous man, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners!"

Pro 23:21 — "For the drunkard and the glutton shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags."

Modern Corruption

An old, plain word for the drunkard; and the drunkard is no antique figure, for our age has made the cup a personality and a comfort.

expand to see more

The live sin to name is the age’s easy friendship with the bottle. Drunkenness is no longer thought a vice but a style: the daily glass held up as a personality, the wine poured to bear the day, the joke that a mother cannot mind her children without it, the young man who measures his manhood by how much he can hold. Scripture is not fooled by the packaging. It counts the winebibber with the glutton and sends both to poverty and rags; it asks who has woe and sorrow and wounds without cause, and answers, they that tarry long at the wine. What the world calls unwinding, the LORD calls a snare, and He warns the son not to look upon the wine when it is red, for the taste that seems harmless is the door to the habit that clothes a man with rags.

The grace that mortifies this sin is not the pledge of the moralist but the fulness of the Spirit. Paul does not merely forbid the cup; he offers a better filling: “be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit” (Eph 5:18). The winebibber drinks to fill an emptiness the wine cannot fill; the answer is a soul filled with Christ, that has no room left for the excess. And there is comfort here for the man already in the ditch: the very name flung as a slander at the sinless Christ is the pledge of his rescue, for the LORD who was called a friend of publicans and sinners is exactly the friend a winebibber needs. He came eating and drinking with such men to save them, and He saves them still.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means a wine-drinker, a tippler, one habitually given to the cup.

expand to see more

Winebibber — wine + bib, “to drink,” from Latin bibere.

It names the habitual drinker, not the man who merely tastes.

Solomon ranks him with the riotous eater of flesh (Pro 23:20).

His end is poverty, drowsiness, and rags (Pro 23:21).

The word was flung as a slander at Christ Himself (Mat 11:19).

Usage

"Be not among winebibbers: the wise man shuns the company of the cup."

"A winebibber is not the man who tastes wine but the man who cannot leave it."

"They called Christ a winebibber — the sinless One who ate with sinners to save them."
